title: Sweetums

jokes.text: Tom's confessional: 'It's a little douchie. Good call, J.' about his new fashion choices while going through a divorce
jokes.setup: Tom announces he's trying to 'up his game' after his divorce
jokes.punchline: He self-describes his own look as 'a little douchie' — with zero remorse or irony, as if this is a reasonable style goal
jokes.explanation: Tom's total lack of self-awareness about being 'a little douchie' is perfectly character-specific. Only Tom would treat this as a neutral descriptor rather than an insult. Strong character integration pulls this above average.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Welcome to Parks and Recreation, where we do important work for the city of Pawnee. I'm Tom Haverford, Director of Parks and Leisure. This department is absolutely douchey.

jokes.text: Tom dismisses Jerry as a fashion advisor: 'Who am I supposed to ask for fashion advice? Jerry? He wears the same soup-stained khakis every day.'
jokes.setup: Tom explains why he needs an outside fashion consultant
jokes.punchline: The specific detail of 'soup-stained khakis every day' — the soup stain makes it perfectly pathetic and specific
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'soup-stained' elevates a standard Jerry-is-a-schlub joke. Jerry as the office punching bag is a running gag, but the detail is doing real work here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, what are you wearing?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? These are my good khakis.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, they're covered in soup stains. That's not fashion advice, that's a cry for help.

jokes.text: Justin calls Tom 'Tommy Timberlake' and says he 'looks like Encyclopedia Brown'
jokes.setup: Justin is acting as Tom's fashion consultant/savior
jokes.punchline: 'Encyclopedia Brown' — the children's detective character — perfectly evokes a nerdy, overeager look that undermines Tom's aspirations to coolness
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Encyclopedia Brown' as the reference is inspired — it's not just 'nerdy,' it evokes a very particular dorky earnestness. The contrast with Tom's self-image makes it land well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My fashion consultant is like if GQ magazine came to life and decided to just roast you for two hours straight.

jokes.text: Tom cycles through absurd accessories: sequined gloves, a cane (dragon vs. serpent), a personalized belt buckle ('What's cracking?'), and an eagle medallion
jokes.setup: Tom is earnestly trying to improve his style after his divorce
jokes.punchline: The accessories escalate from questionable (sequins) to the fully absurd: a custom belt buckle that says 'What's cracking, boo?' and an eagle medallion, all presented with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is peak Tom Haverford character comedy. The escalating list of absurd accessories — each delivered with complete earnestness — works because it's so specific to Tom's deluded self-image. 'Dragon? Serpent?' as a genuine dilemma, and the belt buckle's various personalized greetings, are wonderfully absurd. High character integration score because no other character on this show or most shows would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Fashion Consultant
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm going to call you 'Champ.' You've got real style, Tom. You're like a young Shaft.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Shaft? Really?

dialogue.speaker: Fashion Consultant
dialogue.line: No, wait. You're more of a Veronica Mars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Veronica Mars? She's a girl!

dialogue.speaker: Fashion Consultant
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Tom's eagle medallion and white leather suit exchange: Justin says 'It's horrible.' Tom's friend says 'I like it.'
jokes.setup: Tom models a white leather suit
jokes.punchline: The flat contradiction — 'It's horrible' / 'I like it' — with no winner declared, leaving Tom trapped between two equally useless advisors
jokes.explanation: A functional quick-beat joke. The disagreement is amusing but not particularly crafted — it's a standard 'bad taste' joke with a two-person contradiction structure. Gets the job done.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, what's up? I'm Tom Haverford. Just, you know, keeping it low-key tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This old thing? Nah, it's just a regular shirt. Nothing special about it.

jokes.text: NutriYums commercial: ingredients listed as '100% all-natural corn, a little bit of Sweetums corn syrup, a little drop of sunshine, and some other stuff'
jokes.setup: A promotional video claims NutriYums are a healthy energy bar
jokes.punchline: 'Some other stuff' — the vague, dismissive disclosure after listing corn syrup undercuts the entire health claim and exposes corporate deception with a single phrase
jokes.explanation: 'Some other stuff' is a wonderfully economical punchline. The rhythm builds from reasonable-sounding ingredients to the weasel phrase. Good satirical writing about corporate food deception.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Should I get the mahogany cane or the ebony cane?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, you don't need a cane. You're not old.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's not about age, Jerry. It's about style. A cane is a power accessory.

jokes.text: NutriYums commercial: 'Sorry, Shoelace. We don't make NutriYums for dogs... Yet.'
jokes.setup: The commercial has a dog named Shoelace trying to eat a NutriYum bar
jokes.punchline: 'Yet' — the single word implies the company is actively planning to expand their unhealthy product line to pets, suggesting no ethical limits on their market expansion
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — 'Yet' does all the work. A single word implies an entire corporate cynicism. The structure is perfect: the gentle commercial rejection of the dog, then the ominous pivot. One of the best-constructed jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What's cracking?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What's cracking, baby?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What's cracking, sexy mama?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What's cracking, you beautiful son of a gun?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What's cracking, you absolute unit of human perfection?

jokes.text: Ron's confessional: 'I think the entire government should be privatized. Chuck E. Cheese could run the parks. Everything operated by tokens. Drop in a token, go on the swing set.'
jokes.setup: Ron is commenting on the Sweetums park sponsorship deal
jokes.punchline: Chuck E. Cheese as the model for government — Ron's libertarianism taken to its logical absurd conclusion, with token-operated swings as the vision of ideal governance
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely excellent character comedy. Ron's libertarian philosophy taken to its logical absurd endpoint — Chuck E. Cheese as government — is both a perfect satirical idea and deeply Ron Swanson. The escalation through 'swing set,' 'take a walk,' 'look at a duck' is brilliantly mundane. Could only come from this character. Approaches the 8.0 anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Justin
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm going to be brutally honest with you. That suit is not working.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, this is fire. I look like a sexy snowman.

jokes.text: Ron's escalating token-operated park activities: 'Drop in another token, take a walk. Drop in a token, look at a duck.'
jokes.setup: Ron is describing his Chuck E. Cheese government model
jokes.punchline: The escalation deflates from 'swing set' (an activity) to 'take a walk' to 'look at a duck' — increasingly passive and mundane things to pay for, making the absurdity funnier with each step
jokes.explanation: The deflating escalation to 'look at a duck' is a masterclass in comedic escalation that goes DOWN rather than up in terms of activity scale. 'Look at a duck' is a perfect comedy ending — the duck is the most passive, free, abundantly available park experience imaginable, and Ron wants you to pay for it. Highly quotable. One of the episode's standout jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: A man in a vest is a man with a plan.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That's not true at all.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Look at any historical figure of note. Always wearing a vest.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Most of them were wearing full suits.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The vest was the important part.

jokes.text: Tom to Mark: 'Brendanawicz! Quick question, do you personally know Xzibit? Because I was checking out that pickup truck of yours, and that ride is pimped!'
jokes.setup: Tom approaches Mark with a 'quick question' implying there's something genuine to ask
jokes.punchline: The 'question' is an absurd compliment about the truck being 'pimped' as setup for asking Mark to help him move — the elaborate flattery makes the ulterior motive more transparent
jokes.explanation: The Xzibit/'Pimp My Ride' reference feels slightly dated even for 2010, but Tom's transparent flattery-as-manipulation is in character. The setup/payoff works moderately well.

dialogue.speaker: Nick Newport Jr.
dialogue.line: Does your dog enjoy our delicious Sweetums brand dog food? Well, not yet.

jokes.text: Mark's deadpan response: 'It's really nice of you to compliment my pickup truck with no ulterior motives.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just laid on an elaborate compliment about Mark's truck
jokes.punchline: Mark's flat acknowledgment of the transparent manipulation — 'with no ulterior motives' — delivered as if accepting a genuine compliment
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical deadpan. Mark's weariness with Tom's manipulations is well-expressed in a single line. The structure is tight — the irony lands immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not against parks. I'm just saying they'd be more efficient if they were privately run. You could monetize every aspect.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Want to walk on the grass? That'll be fifty cents. Looking at ducks? A dollar. Breathing the fresh air? Two dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Sitting on a bench? That's five dollars. And if you want to actually feed the ducks, well, you need to purchase a special duck-feeding license for twenty-five dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Smiling at nature? That's going to cost you. We'd have vendors everywhere collecting payments. The government couldn't run anything this efficiently.

jokes.text: Mark's confessional: 'I (fucking) hate having a pickup truck.'
jokes.setup: Mark has just been guilted into helping Tom move
jokes.punchline: The blunt, profane confessional — the universally relatable truth of truck ownership making you the default mover — delivered with flat resignation
jokes.explanation: A highly relatable, economical punchline to the sequence. The profanity is earns its place through the flat resignation. Not a novel observation but delivered with perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, that's a nice truck, Mark. Did Xzibit pimp it out?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: What? No. I just... bought it like this.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mmmhmm, sure you did.

jokes.text: Mark admits: 'I'm totally blanking on a valid excuse right now, so, yes. I'll help you.'
jokes.setup: Tom has asked Mark to help him move, and Mark doesn't want to
jokes.punchline: Mark admits with complete honesty that he can't think of a way out — inverting the social norm of making up excuses by just stating the truth of his predicament
jokes.explanation: Smart subversion — instead of inventing an excuse, Mark simply admits defeat with blunt honesty. The deadpan transparency is characteristic of the show's brand of comedy and of Mark specifically. Well-constructed in few words.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark, you are the most talented, intelligent, and physically attractive man I have ever met.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: What do you want?

jokes.text: Andy immediately volunteers to help Tom move: 'Can I help you move? I'm really good at it. Afterwards, I'll take the cardboard from the boxes and use it for break dancing.'
jokes.setup: Tom is asking for moving help
jokes.punchline: Andy's enthusiasm + the completely unprompted addition of break dancing cardboard as a personal benefit reveals his childlike priorities — he's excited about the cardboard, not helping Tom
jokes.explanation: The break-dancing cardboard detail is perfectly Andy — it shows his enthusiastic naivety and reveals his actual motivation is self-serving in an entirely innocent, childlike way. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Mark, can you help me move? I need to borrow your truck.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Yeah, sure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Great! We can take the Mark-mobile!

jokes.text: April's reversal — she agrees to help after previously saying she'd 'rather watch a sex tape of her grandparents'
jokes.setup: Andy reveals April initially refused help by citing she'd rather watch her grandparents' sex tape
jokes.punchline: April's reversal ('Shut up. I don't have anything else to do. Do you want help or not?') preserves her disaffected persona while the sex-tape detail is the actual joke — the hyperbolic disgust she'd prefer over helping
jokes.explanation: The sex tape detail is a great April line — dark and specific in a way that's perfectly in character. Her reversal while maintaining face is also good April behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'd love to help Tom move, but I can't think of an excuse.

jokes.text: Ann's response to the grandparents sex tape revelation: 'I think that that's really, really sweet, that your grandparents still make love.'
jokes.setup: April's grandparents sex tape has just been mentioned as a negative
jokes.punchline: Ann reframes it as wholesome and romantic — her earnest, nurse-brain framing of the darkest possible scenario as 'really sweet' is perfect Ann
jokes.explanation: Ann's earnest reframe of April's disgusted hypothetical as a touching sign of elderly love is a great character-specific response. It's unexpected and lands because it's so genuinely Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I agreed to help Tom move. I didn't think about it. I just said yes. Now I'm realizing I have to spend my Saturday helping Tom move into some apartment that probably has a weird smell and is filled with his stupid furniture that he bought at some discount warehouse.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: And of course Tom's going to want to borrow my truck. Everyone always wants to borrow my truck. 'Hey Mark, can I use your truck? Hey Mark, my truck's in the shop, can I borrow yours?' No. Get your own truck.

jokes.text: Leslie produces a blood-alcohol chart to stop Ron from driving: 'What are you, 5'11", 210 pounds, three whiskeys? Looks like you are just over the line into impaired.'
jokes.setup: Ron insists he's fine to drive after drinking
jokes.punchline: Leslie has been carrying a blood-alcohol chart at all times and can immediately assess Ron's impairment by weight and drink count — the absurd preparedness is quintessential Leslie
jokes.explanation: Leslie's obsessive preparedness — carrying a BAC chart — is perfect character integration. The deadpan clinical assessment ('just over the line into impaired') is delivered with Leslie's characteristic earnest efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'll help you move! I'm really strong and I've got great cardio from all my breakdancing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Plus, you're gonna have all those cardboard boxes lying around, right? That's basically free breakdancing equipment.

jokes.text: Ron notices the back of Leslie's BAC chart: 'And on the back, it teaches you how to play blackjack.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just used a blood-alcohol chart to assess Ron's sobriety
jokes.punchline: The chart doubles as a blackjack guide — the mundane dual-purpose of the novelty chart undercuts the seriousness of the intervention in a perfectly deadpan way
jokes.explanation: A great quick beat. The BAC chart/blackjack guide combo is a specific, absurd detail that feels real (like a gas station purchase). It extends the joke about Leslie's unusual accessories while being its own punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, you volunteering? That's amazing!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, well... I'm here now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This is so great! What made you want to help?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ben said if I didn't come, he'd tell everyone about the time I cried at a dog food commercial.

jokes.text: Ron's claim: 'Swansons have a preternaturally high tolerance for alcohol. My old man used to put Wild Turkey on his Corn Flakes.'
jokes.setup: Ron is arguing he doesn't need to wait to drive because of his natural tolerance
jokes.punchline: 'Wild Turkey on his Corn Flakes' — the specific brand and the specific breakfast item make this land as a real family tradition rather than an exaggeration, which is funnier
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest jokes. 'Wild Turkey on his Corn Flakes' is deeply specific in a way that makes it feel like genuine Swanson family mythology rather than a generic 'my family drinks a lot' joke. The word 'preternaturally' — Ron's unexpectedly elevated vocabulary — adds another layer. The specificity (brand + food) is what separates this from a 3-star joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's actually really sweet. Your grandparents still have that spark, you know? I think that's beautiful. I hope me and my future wife are still doing that when we're old.

jokes.text: Ron, bored waiting for the BAC to drop, reads the blackjack instructions aloud: 'Insurance is a side bet when you wager half of your original bet because you believe the dealer has a 10 in the hole.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron are waiting an hour for Ron to sober up; Ron is reading the back of the BAC chart
jokes.punchline: Ron, a proud, capable man, is reduced to reading blackjack instructions off a novelty chart to pass time — the visual of Ron Swanson carefully studying this is inherently funny
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the blackjack chart, with the comedy being the image of Ron Swanson earnestly absorbing blackjack strategy from a novelty DUI card. Works better as a visual than in transcript.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, can you drive?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a precise calculation. I've made a chart.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A chart of what?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Blood alcohol content versus my ability to operate a vehicle. According to my data, I'm actually a better driver after exactly four whiskeys.

jokes.text: Ron, clearly fed up with waiting, shouts at Leslie: 'Get off my car, woman!'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron have been sitting awkwardly for a long time waiting for his BAC to drop
jokes.punchline: Ron's patience has entirely collapsed — 'Get off my car, woman!' is an eruption that confirms he's been bottling irritation, and the blunt address of 'woman' is perfectly Ron
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — four words capture Ron's entire relationship with Leslie's interference. The word 'woman' delivered in Ron's growl is deeply character-specific and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, what is this chart?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a blood alcohol content reference guide. You can use it to determine how many drinks you can safely have based on your body weight and—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I see. And what is this section here at the bottom?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's blackjack instructions.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you put blackjack instructions on a blood alcohol chart?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because if you're drunk enough to need this chart, you're probably drunk enough to want to play blackjack.

jokes.text: Leslie responds to Ron's outburst: 'Twenty minutes.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just yelled 'Get off my car, woman!'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's flat, clinical 'Twenty minutes' — completely ignoring his frustration and just reporting the remaining wait time — is perfect Leslie Knope energy
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum payoff. Leslie's complete imperviousness to Ron's irritation, responding only with the remaining wait time, is perfectly in character and extremely well-timed. Economy score of 10 — it couldn't be shorter.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My father put whiskey on my cereal when I was a boy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's why I can drink so much without getting drunk.

jokes.text: Ron's reflection on the blackjack chart: 'The dealer really has an advantage. That's what I get the most from this.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been reading the blackjack instructions while waiting
jokes.punchline: Ron's takeaway from an involuntary waiting period is a genuine observation about blackjack strategy — his complete diversion from the actual situation into useful information is very Ron
jokes.explanation: A nice close to the blackjack chart running bit. Ron processing real takeaways from a novelty item while in an awkward situation is character-specific and funny. Closes the bit well.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I made this after drinking an entire bottle of scotch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's a birdhouse. Dovetail joints, mortise and tenon construction, hand-planed wood.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea how I did that.

jokes.text: Ron reveals he went home and crafted a small harp using a band saw, spoke shave and oscillating spindle sander — and brought photographs of himself drinking whiskey with yesterday's newspaper as proof
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Ron had a good night after their parking lot standoff
jokes.punchline: Ron made a harp AND documented his whiskey drinking with newspaper-verified photos like a hostage proof — the combination of artisan craftwork and meticulous documentation of debauchery is deeply specific Ron Swanson behavior
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke. The harp + whiskey combination is quintessential Ron Swanson — he has the skills of a 19th century frontiersman AND the drinking of one. But 'here are photographs of me drinking the whiskey. You'll notice I'm holding up yesterday's newspaper, so you can tell that I'm not lying' takes it to another level. The hostage-proof methodology applied to recreational drinking is original, specific, deeply in character, and has remarkable structure. Could only be Ron. One of the series' great Ron Swanson moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have nothing to hide. Here's photographic evidence of my drinking.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Today's newspaper. My whiskey. My face. Proof of life.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to the harp and whiskey photos: 'I feel like I'm in a spa.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just presented a harp he built and newspaper-verified whiskey photos
jokes.punchline: Leslie's utterly non-sequitur spa comparison — she apparently finds Ron's masculine intensity calming and relaxing, which is an unexpected and funny response
jokes.explanation: A perfect reaction beat. The non-sequitur of 'spa' applied to Ron's Hemingway-esque display is both surprising and reveals something true about Leslie's affectionate relationship with Ron's character. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark, where's all your moving equipment? Dolly, hand truck, something?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I don't own a dolly, Tom. I'm a 40-year-old man who lives alone and has accepted that.

jokes.text: Mark's exasperation about moving supplies: 'Ooh, I thought the mover supplied those.' / 'I'm not a mover! I'm a sap who owns a truck.'
jokes.setup: Mark asks Tom if he has furniture pads and dollies
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a sap who owns a truck' — the self-identification as a 'sap' is both self-pitying and accurate, a perfect encapsulation of the universal truck-owner burden
jokes.explanation: Builds on the established pickup truck running gag. 'I'm a sap who owns a truck' is a quotable self-assessment that extends the joke with a new angle. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: These energy bars are terrific!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, they're terrible, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, I'm pretty sure they're terrific.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Jerry, terrific means good.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know what terrific means, Andy. And these bars are it.

jokes.text: Jerry's NutriYum debate: 'They are terrific.' / 'Terrific's not more than amazing, Jerry.' / 'No? Well, it's not less.'
jokes.setup: Characters are debating the quality of NutriYums; Jerry says they're 'terrific'
jokes.punchline: Jerry's gentle semantic defense — 'it's not less' — is both pathetically reasonable and perfectly Jerry: he can't even win a word choice argument
jokes.explanation: The semantic quibble is a perfect micro-joke. Jerry's mild rebuttal ('well, it's not less') captures his character — he can't assert himself, but he's technically correct, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Krackel bars are basically healthy. They're mostly rice.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Rice doesn't make candy healthy, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, it should.

jokes.text: Someone defends Krackel bars: 'It's not that crazy. Krackel bars, also healthy and delicious.' / 'No, they're not.' / 'Yeah. They actually have rice in them. So...'
jokes.setup: Ann says she can't believe NutriYums are healthy
jokes.punchline: Tom's reasoning that rice in Krackel bars makes them healthy — the logical leap that a grain component = health food — and the dismissive 'So...' trailing off as if the point is made
jokes.explanation: The 'so...' trailing off after dubious nutritional logic is a good joke structure — the speaker clearly knows the argument is weak but presses on. Tom's nutritional reasoning is in character with his generally misinformed confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, you can't just eat bacon and think it's a vegetable because it comes from a pig and pigs eat vegetables.

jokes.text: Someone (likely Ben or Chris) to Andy after he eats 100 NutriYums: 'Andy, you're fine, but you're simple.'
jokes.setup: Andy has eaten an absurd number of energy bars and seems perfectly happy about it
jokes.punchline: 'You're fine, but you're simple' — the gentle, clinical assessment of Andy's intellect, delivered without malice, is perfectly honest and funny
jokes.explanation: Extremely economical — six words perfectly describe Andy Dwyer. The construction is perfect: 'you're fine' affirms him before the actual observation. It's kind and devastating simultaneously, which is very Parks and Rec in tone.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, these energy bars are gonna change your life. They're packed with nutrients, they taste amazing, and they'll give you the energy you need to get through the day.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm not really interested in energy bars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, that's the thing. Looking at you, I'd say you could use all the help you can get. These bars will really... improve things. Visually, I mean. For you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Are you seriously trying to insult me into buying your energy bars?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Is it working?

jokes.text: Tom greets Ann with: 'Ann! Oh! Look at you! You're looking pretty unhealthy today. You might need one of these, NutriYum, by Sweetums.'
jokes.setup: Tom is in a sugar-rush enthusiasm for NutriYums
jokes.punchline: Tom's completely fabricated concern about Ann's health as a pretext to sell/promote the very product Ann is about to debunk — the absurdity of calling Ann 'unhealthy' while in a sugar high
jokes.explanation: Functional joke that sets up Ann's debunking, but not particularly crafted. Tom's sugar-rush enthusiasm is a good character state but the specific joke is average.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: These energy bars are completely healthy. They have all the nutrients you need.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, they're 90% sugar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Oprah endorsed them, so...

jokes.text: Ann debunks NutriYums: 'No, they're not, they're terrible for you.' / Tom: 'No, they're not. There's a picture of Lance Armstrong on there.'
jokes.setup: Ann says NutriYums are terrible for you
jokes.punchline: Tom's rebuttal is that Lance Armstrong's endorsement photo proves health — a perfect encapsulation of how meaningless celebrity endorsements are and how easily Tom is persuaded by surface signals
jokes.explanation: The Lance Armstrong endorsement-as-proof joke is decent satire of celebrity health marketing. Tom's complete credulity is in character. Note: in hindsight this joke has a dark irony given Armstrong's later doping scandal, which slightly increases its dark-comedy value in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm getting involved because these issues matter to me.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We need to address the challenges, the obstacles, the complications, the difficulties, the problems, and frankly, the chunk monsters in this community.

jokes.text: Ann on the ingredients: 'High-fructose corn syrup, corn syrup.' / 'There's only eight grams of fat. / 'Yeah. Per serving. A bar is four servings.'
jokes.setup: Tom points to eight grams of fat as evidence NutriYums aren't that bad
jokes.punchline: 'A bar is four servings' — the classic nutritional label deception, landing as a direct hit on food marketing tactics
jokes.explanation: A real and relatable point about nutritional labels done well dramatically but not originally — this is an observational joke about a well-known consumer frustration. The setup/payoff structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Librarian
dialogue.line: Well, actually, libraries are still very important institutions.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh really? Because the last time I checked, Google exists. So unless you're planning to alphabetize the entire internet, I think we're good.

jokes.text: Ann explains the 'happy crowd' is on a sugar rush: 'Yeah, that's a sugar rush.' / 'They're gonna crash soon, and it's not gonna be pretty.' / 'Yeah, I'm gonna crash soon, too. 'Cause I've eaten, like, 40 of these.'
jokes.setup: Tom points to the happy crowd as evidence the bars are good
jokes.punchline: Tom admits he's also going to crash — and has eaten 40 bars — undercutting his own defense of the product while confirming Ann's point
jokes.explanation: Tom inadvertently proving Ann's point through self-incrimination is a nice comedic structure. The escalation from 40 to an earlier 100 bars creates a running thread of absurd overconsumption.

dialogue.speaker: Marcia
dialogue.line: Oh my, someone checked out 'How to Identify and Treat Hemorrhoids'.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not mine!

jokes.text: Ann's confessional about Pawnee obesity: 'The kids here are beefy. They're just husky, big-boned, plus-sized chunk monsters.'
jokes.setup: Ann notes Pawnee is the fourth most obese city in America
jokes.punchline: The escalating euphemisms — 'beefy,' 'husky,' 'big-boned,' 'plus-sized chunk monsters' — the last of which completely abandons any pretense of delicacy
jokes.explanation: The escalation from socially acceptable euphemisms to 'chunk monsters' is perfectly structured — each term is funnier than the last, and 'chunk monsters' is a great coinage. The final phrase completely abandons political correctness after a pretense of sensitivity. 'Chunk monsters' is quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget the Dewey Decimal System! It's more like the Dewey Decimal Nightmare!

jokes.text: Ann adds: 'I call them like I see them.'
jokes.setup: Ann has just called Pawnee children 'chunk monsters'
jokes.punchline: The self-congratulatory 'I call them like I see them' after an escalating list of fat-shaming terms — Ann's complete lack of awareness that this is unusual
jokes.explanation: Good button on the previous joke. The self-satisfied coda after 'chunk monsters' adds a layer by making Ann oblivious to the inappropriateness of what she just said.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, don't you care about the health and well-being of our citizens?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. I don't care about people's health. And I don't think the government should be involved in people's health decisions. If someone wants to smoke a cigarette, they should be allowed to smoke a cigarette. If someone wants to drink a beer, they should be allowed to drink a beer. The government has no right to tell people what to do.

jokes.text: Leslie feeds Ann almonds: 'Let's get some almonds in you, okay?' — Ann struggles and can't open the bag: 'I can't open them.'
jokes.setup: Ann is already crashing from the sugar rush of NutriYums
jokes.punchline: The sugar crash has left Ann incapacitated to the point where she can't open an almond bag — a comic physical payoff to the sugar rush setup
jokes.explanation: A nice quick physical beat. The almond bag incapacity is a fun payoff to the sugar crash foreshadowing, though it's relatively minor.

dialogue.speaker: Paul
dialogue.line: Why do you keep calling sidebars?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you keep doing things that require sidebars!

dialogue.speaker: Paul
dialogue.line: What things?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what things. You wore a turtleneck to my house.

jokes.text: Ann at the library: 'I hate it here. This place is evil.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are researching NutriYums at the public library
jokes.punchline: The library is treated as an evil place — this is a running joke in Parks and Rec about the Parks/Library departmental rivalry, with Ann's blanket condemnation being the absurd escalation
jokes.explanation: Part of the show's Parks-vs-Libraries running mythology. Ann's simple 'This place is evil' is perfectly deadpan and works well as setup for the confrontational librarian scene.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So there's this Canadian version of the movie where all the dialogue is rapped.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's called 'The Maple Leaf Remix.'

jokes.text: Librarian Marci insults Leslie: 'Are they finally teaching you Parks people how to read? Oh, I guess not. It's a movie.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann arrive at the library to find old Sweetums promotional videos
jokes.punchline: The librarian takes the opportunity to mock the Parks Department's literacy, then realizes it's a movie — inadvertently undermining her own insult
jokes.explanation: Good use of the Parks/Library rivalry that's a recurring element of the show. The self-defeating insult structure is well-constructed — she undermines her own snob attack. The rivalry gives extra context for comedy savvy viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Welcome to my bedroom. As you can see, I've spared no expense. Italian marble floors, a bed made from the finest Egyptian cotton, and a closet that's basically a small department store.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I also have a sauna, a steam room, and a personal masseuse on call 24/7. And that's just the entryway.

jokes.text: Leslie to the librarian Marci: 'You're pretty cocky for someone whose job is obsolete because of the Internet.'
jokes.setup: The librarian Marci has been condescending to Leslie, asking if 'Parks people' are learning to read
jokes.punchline: Leslie's comeback — that librarians are obsolete due to the Internet — is both a sharp retort and funny because it comes from Leslie, who is usually the target of such put-downs and is clearly delighted to have a good comeback
jokes.explanation: Leslie landing a good comeback is funny because she's usually the one being condescended to and she's relishing it. The 'obsolete because of the Internet' line is sharp and specific to the librarian context.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is DJ Roomba. It's a Roomba with a mini DJ setup on top of it. So it cleans your floor while simultaneously DJing your party.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've been working on the name. I'm thinking either 'The Dust- turner' or 'Roombarton Barton'... no, I like DJ Roomba better.

jokes.text: Marci reveals: 'You seem to have a $40 late fee on a book called Mysteries of the Female Orgasm.'
jokes.setup: Marci is processing Leslie and Ann's library cards; Leslie has just insulted her
jokes.punchline: Ann has a $40 late fee on a book called 'Mysteries of the Female Orgasm' — the specific embarrassing title, the dollar amount, and the public revelation work together
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe/embarrassment comedy. The book title is specific and embarrassing in the right way — it's not gratuitously vulgar but it's genuinely awkward. The timing (as retaliation for Leslie's insult) is structurally satisfying. '$40 late fee' adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo, check it out. We got DJ Roomba in the house!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's what I'm talking about. Keep it spinning, baby. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

jokes.text: Ann's flat denial and then immediate flight: 'No, I don't.' / 'Yeah, you do.' / 'Ann, grab the movie! Go, go, go, go!'
jokes.setup: Marci has just announced Ann's embarrassing late fee publicly
jokes.punchline: Ann's denial is immediately contradicted, and Leslie's escape plan ('Go go go!') suggests they're fleeing rather than paying — confirming the embarrassment and adding physical comedy
jokes.explanation: The escape escalates the cringe comedy nicely. Leslie's 'go go go' heist energy applied to fleeing a library is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I think it's beautiful. People have the right to make their own choices about what they put in their bodies, even if those choices lead to their death.

jokes.text: Leslie's parting shot: 'Punk-ass book jockeys!'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are fleeing the library
jokes.punchline: 'Punk-ass book jockeys' — Leslie's improvised insult for librarians is gloriously specific and absurd, made funnier by the fact that she's running away while yelling it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Punk-ass book jockeys' is an original coinage that somehow feels both perfectly Leslie (passionate about government/civic institutions) and completely out of character (she'd normally never say 'punk-ass'). The compound insult is original, highly quotable, and the context of yelling it while fleeing makes it perfect. Approaches 8.5 anchor quality — it's memorable, character-specific, and genuinely funny as a standalone phrase.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Sugar is terrible for you. It rots your teeth, it makes you fat, it causes diabetes.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: But it tastes so good!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's because God wants you to die.

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ron for a 'sidebar' to discuss NutriYums; Ron refuses to engage: 'I don't care. We're doing it.' / Leslie: 'That's a... we're in a sidebar.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to have a private conversation with Ron during a meeting
jokes.punchline: Ron refuses to honor the social convention of a sidebar — 'I don't care. We're doing it' — delivered in the middle of the sidebar, making the sidebar immediately pointless
jokes.explanation: Ron's refusal to play by procedural rules is very in character. The failed sidebar structure is a clean comedic bit, though not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: Is corn syrup really that bad for you?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, actually, corn syrup comes from corn, which is a vegetable, so it's basically health food.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Corn isn't a vegetable, Jerry. It's a grain.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm pretty sure corn is a fruit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's definitely not a fruit, Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, what about corn on the cob? That's basically a vegetable.

jokes.text: Escalating sidebar chaos: Leslie asks Paul for a sidebar, Paul refuses. Then Leslie explains to Paul in a sidebar that Ron is upset about the drunk driving chart — Ron: 'Stop sidebarring.'
jokes.setup: Leslie keeps requesting sidebars to manage the meeting
jokes.punchline: The sidebar meta-joke escalates: Leslie uses a sidebar to explain a previous sidebar, while Ron — who violated the first sidebar — now tells everyone to stop sidebarring
jokes.explanation: The escalating sidebar bit builds nicely into a running gag. Ron's 'Stop sidebarring' is the payoff — the man who refused to respect the sidebar now enforcing it is a nice ironic turn.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: I just wanted to say that you have really nice... um... healthcare policies.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: And I think we should all get together sometime. For health reasons.

jokes.text: Leslie whispers to Paul: 'Ron's upset because I didn't let him drive last night.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to explain Ron's grouchiness through a 'sidebar' with Paul
jokes.punchline: Leslie treats the drunk driving incident as personal drama to gossip about — reducing Ron's principled behavior to a petty grievance, and doing so in a whisper that Ron can clearly still hear
jokes.explanation: A decent callback to the parking lot scene, reframing Ron's previous night as office gossip. The whisper-that-Ron-can-hear structure is a classic cringe beat.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: What about something healthier?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Bacon.

dialogue.speaker: Multiple Citizens
dialogue.line: Bacon! Bacon! Bacon!

jokes.text: Tom discovers Mark hasn't packed yet: 'You said it was just odds and ends.' / 'It is, yeah. And some furniture. And the plasma TV. You haven't even folded up the boxes yet.'
jokes.setup: Mark and friends have arrived to help Tom move
jokes.punchline: The escalating revelation of what 'odds and ends' includes — furniture, plasma TV, unfolded boxes — Tom has done nothing to prepare
jokes.explanation: A relatable escalation of the 'small favor that isn't small' comedy. Functional and character-consistent for Tom, but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Nobody touches my car. Nobody. I don't care if we're moving to a new office or a new planet.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Donna, we need to coordinate the trucks. Can you help organize—

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Mark, that's what you're here for. I'm making sure my Lexus gets there in one piece. You handle the rest.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: But I have to load my own desk and—

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Mark. My car. Your problem. Figure it out.

jokes.text: Andy discovers Deep Blue Sea on DVD: 'Dude, Deep Blue Sea. Greatest movie ever made. That's the Canadian version, 22 extra minutes, and there's a bonus audio track where LL Cool J raps all his dialog.'
jokes.setup: Mark is trying to get everyone to pack Tom's boxes
jokes.punchline: The Canadian Deep Blue Sea DVD with LL Cool J rapping all his dialogue — a completely absurd 'special feature' that Andy treats as a completely real and desirable thing. The specificity makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Andy joke. The specific detail of LL Cool J rapping all his own dialogue is an inspired absurdist invention — it's not just 'Andy likes a dumb movie,' it's a specific, vivid absurdity that Andy treats with complete sincerity. The Canadian edition angle adds another layer. One of the episode's standout jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Nick Newport Sr.
dialogue.line: Here at Sweetums, we've perfected the art of animal fattening. We take lean livestock and through the power of corn syrup, we transform them into plump, juicy specimens ready for your dinner table. It's the same process we use on our consumers. I mean, customers.

jokes.text: Tom reveals his walk-in closet is actually 'a walk-in closet/home fitness center'
jokes.setup: Mark and April are impressed by the large room
jokes.punchline: It's a hybrid walk-in closet/home fitness center — the slash combination is funny because it implies both are partial and probably neither is functional
jokes.explanation: A decent setup for the DJ Roomba reveal. The closet/gym hybrid is a funny Tom Haverford luxury that implies he uses neither space properly.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Dude, we're not here to help you move.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? Why are you here then?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: We came to watch April tell you what a terrible job you're doing.

jokes.text: Tom reveals DJ Roomba: 'I strapped an MP3 player to one of those floor cleaning robots. I call him "DJ Roomba." Little guy cruises around and plays music.'
jokes.setup: Tom's room contains an unusual device
jokes.punchline: DJ Roomba — a Roomba with an MP3 player — treated by Tom as a genuine technological achievement and a beloved companion ('little guy')
jokes.explanation: DJ Roomba is an iconic Parks and Rec invention. The concept is perfect: Tom's love of technology, music, and unnecessary gadgets combined in a thing that is both completely useless and entirely delightful. 'Little guy cruises around and plays music' is Tom's sincere pride in his creation. This is one of the series' best character-specific inventions. The naming ('DJ Roomba') and affection ('little guy') elevate it to near-iconic status. Fully justifies a score at the top of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'd like to order a large pizza. And, uh, make sure it's brown and spicy... like me.

dialogue.speaker: Pizza Worker
dialogue.line: ...What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just put extra pepperoni on it.

jokes.text: Tom about DJ Roomba: 'He likes me.' / 'Let's dance for a little while, Mark.'
jokes.setup: DJ Roomba is playing music as everyone watches
jokes.punchline: Tom's sincere claim that the Roomba 'likes him' — projecting emotions onto an appliance — combined with inviting Mark to dance instead of pack
jokes.explanation: The emotional bond Tom has formed with an appliance ('He likes me') is a great comedic detail. The invitation to dance instead of pack is peak Tom prioritization.

dialogue.speaker: Nick Newport Sr.
dialogue.line: Son of a bitch!

jokes.text: Ron's confessional on freedom to eat badly: 'The whole point of this country is, if you want to eat garbage, balloon up to 600 pounds and die of a heart attack at 43, you can. You are free to do so. To me, that's beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Ron is commenting on Leslie's opposition to NutriYums
jokes.punchline: 'To me, that's beautiful' — Ron's reverent, sincere conclusion that dying of a preventable heart attack at 43 represents the ideal of American freedom is the absurdist endpoint of his libertarianism
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best Ron Swanson speeches. The specific age (43) and weight (600 pounds) make it vivid rather than generic. 'To me, that's beautiful' delivered with complete sincerity is perfect. This is Ron Swanson's philosophy expressed at its most absurd and most pure — it could only be him, and it perfectly satirizes extreme libertarianism while being genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Town hall question: 'If sugar is so bad, how come Jesus made it taste so good?'
jokes.setup: Ann is giving a health presentation about the dangers of sugar
jokes.punchline: A citizen's theological defense of sugar — 'Jesus made it taste good, therefore it's fine' — is perfect Pawnee-citizen logic, revealing the town's unique combination of religiosity and nutritional ignorance
jokes.explanation: A great Pawnee-citizen joke. The theological sugar defense is original, economical, and perfectly captures the show's portrayal of Pawnee as a town of wonderfully unreasonable people. It also works as pure absurdist logic. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, everyone, we're going to have a completely fair and unbiased vote. Option one: we adopt my plan, which is brilliant and will save the town. Option two: we do nothing and let the town die.

jokes.text: Citizen's claim: 'But isn't all food bad for you? I've been eating lasagna and muffins every day of my life for 40 years and I feel terrible.'
jokes.setup: Ann is presenting health information at the town hall
jokes.punchline: The citizen argues 'all food is bad for you' using as evidence the fact that eating only lasagna and muffins makes him feel terrible — the conclusion is the wrong takeaway from clearly correct data
jokes.explanation: The inverted logic — using evidence of a bad diet to argue all food is bad — is excellent. The specificity of 'lasagna and muffins every day for 40 years' is perfect Pawnee citizen detail. The structure is tight: self-defeating argument delivered without self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I've got it. What if we move to London for six months, then to Paris for three months, then back to Pawnee, but just for weekends?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the worst idea I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Or—or we could move to a boat. We'd just be constantly moving. Problem solved.

jokes.text: Citizen defends corn syrup: 'What's so bad about corn syrup? It's natural. Corn's a fruit. Syrup comes from a bush.'
jokes.setup: Ann is explaining the dangers of high-fructose corn syrup
jokes.punchline: 'Corn's a fruit. Syrup comes from a bush.' — both claims are wrong, delivered with absolute confidence. The cascading false facts have a beautiful escalating wrongness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Corn's a fruit. Syrup comes from a bush.' is a perfect comedy construction — two confident wrong claims delivered in rapid succession, with 'syrup comes from a bush' being especially absurd. The citizen's confidence in completely fabricated botany is hilarious. Highly quotable. Approaches the episode's best material.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Dude, Andy's like, so not chill. He probably listens to like, Nickelback or something.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yeah bro, and I bet he does like, CrossFit or goes to SoulCycle or something lame like that.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Dude, he probably thinks Silly Bandz are still cool. What a loser.

jokes.text: A male citizen tries to get Ann's number by saying his friend thinks she's cute: 'How do we know you're really a nurse?' — then attempts to get her e-mail — 'I just got on AOL.'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to give a serious health presentation at the town hall
jokes.punchline: A citizen attempts to get Ann's number by claiming his friend thinks she's cute, then pivots to email — 'I just got on AOL' — the AOL detail in 2010 is perfect: this man is charmingly oblivious and years behind the internet
jokes.explanation: The 'I just got on AOL' detail is the real punchline here — a perfectly specific period detail that makes the citizen feel real and pathetic in a charming way. The escalation from friend's number to email is good cringe structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. So you're saying that if I sleep with a man, that makes me gay?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But what if I think about a woman the whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wouldn't that make it straight?

jokes.text: Crowd chants: 'Ham and mayonnaise! Ham and mayonnaise!' — demanding they throw out the NutriYums and eat ham-and-mayo sandwiches instead
jokes.setup: A citizen suggests replacing NutriYums with ham-and-mayonnaise sandwiches; Ann says that's not a good idea
jokes.punchline: The crowd breaks into a chant for ham-and-mayonnaise — the specific sandwich as a rallying cry, the fact that this is the crowd's preferred health alternative, and the absurdity of a civic chant about sandwich ingredients
jokes.explanation: A great crowd comedy moment. 'Ham and mayonnaise' as a chant works because it's so specific and so wrong as a health alternative. The crowd's enthusiasm for this particular sandwich — delivered as a political rally — is perfect Pawnee behavior. The repetition as a chant is inherently funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What are you eating?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Meat and eggs. Bacon, steak, a whole roasted chicken. And I'm washing it down with Scotch and a cigar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's called the Swanson. I invented it. You can't have any.

jokes.text: Leslie's reflection: 'I'm actually encouraged. The questions were more relevant than usual.'
jokes.setup: The town hall has devolved into a ham-and-mayo sandwich chant
jokes.punchline: Leslie's genuine encouragement at questions she considers 'more relevant than usual' — the bar for relevance in Pawnee is apparently lower than the ham-and-mayo chant suggests
jokes.explanation: Leslie's optimism in the face of obvious disaster is a core character note, and 'more relevant than usual' implies previous meetings have been even worse — which is funnier than the current chaos. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you can't keep eating like this. You're going to die.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not fine! I've actually already written your eulogy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, let's hear it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's really good.

jokes.text: Ann is ordering shoes: 'Yeah, I need to order the brown Timberlands in a size eight, narrow. How much is the next-day shipping? And, what's two-day shipping?' Then orders pad thai: 'And, I'd like to place an order for one pad thai, chicken, and no scallions on it, please. Just for one person, yeah. Just one.'
jokes.setup: Ann appears to be on an important phone call after the town hall
jokes.punchline: Ann is shopping for shoes and ordering solo pad thai — 'just for one person, yeah. Just one' — the lonely solo order, juxtaposed with the fact that Mark is moving out and Wendy is presumably nearby, implies Ann is processing romantic disappointment through consumer comfort
jokes.explanation: 'Just for one person, yeah. Just one' is a great small moment — the emphasis on aloneness, the slight over-explanation, perfectly captures lonely self-comfort. The juxtaposition with shoe shopping adds a layer of sad-funny relatable behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron's eulogy was basically a swan song. Or as I like to call it... a Swanson song.

jokes.text: Donna refuses to let anything be put in her car: 'Uh-uh. That's it. My baby has a delicate suspension.' — then insists Mark put heavy items in his truck anyway
jokes.setup: The movers need Donna's car to transport Tom's heavy items
jokes.punchline: Donna protects her car with 'delicate suspension' but has no problem passing the burden to Mark's truck — her total unsympathetic selfishness about her vehicle is great Donna character comedy
jokes.explanation: Donna's fierce protection of her car is an established character trait and 'delicate suspension' is a good specific detail. The pivot to immediately demanding Mark's truck take the load is solid character-comedy structure.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Hey April, want to go rollerblading with me this weekend?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Come on, it'll be fun. I used to be really good at it.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I mean, I'm a little heavier now, so I mostly just... roll downhill and try to remember how to stop.

jokes.text: Tom discovers his pocket squares have been damaged: 'Ah! My pocket squares!'
jokes.setup: Moving items are being loaded and something has been damaged
jokes.punchline: Tom's most prized possessions being 'pocket squares' — the anguished cry implies they're among his most treasured possessions, which is perfectly Tom
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat. The pocket squares as Tom's crisis object is funny and specific to his character, though it's a brief moment without much craft beyond the character insight.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I don't fall. I'm very coordinated on rollerblades.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: *falls*

jokes.text: Nick Newport Jr. casually references 'Shoelace' again at the community meeting — Leslie notes 'Shoelace couldn't make it.' — Nick: 'Aw!'
jokes.setup: Nick Newport Jr. has arrived at the community meeting
jokes.punchline: Nick's immediate concern for his dog Shoelace's attendance at a corporate accountability meeting — and his genuine disappointment the dog didn't come — is absurd and reveals the CEO's priorities
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Shoelace commercial bit. Nick's genuine disappointment about the dog not being there humanizes and absurdifies him simultaneously. The callback structure works.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, you broke DJ Roomba. So here's what's gonna happen. When I die, I'm gonna come back and haunt you. And you know what I'm gonna do? I'm gonna follow you around playing nothing but Nickelback for all eternity.

jokes.text: Old Sweetums promotional video: 'Cheap, delicious, sugary corn is currently being used by farms to fatten up their cows and pigs. Look how fat those cows are! Fat, happy and docile, the way we like them.'
jokes.setup: Leslie plays a vintage Sweetums promotional video from 30 years ago to undercut the modern company's health claims
jokes.punchline: 'Fat, happy and docile, the way we like them' — the company's own video explicitly describes fattening livestock with the same ingredient they claim is healthy for humans, with the CEO's obvious pleasure at the 'docile' cows
jokes.explanation: 'Fat, happy and docile, the way we like them' is darkly funny as self-incriminating corporate language. The parallel between fattening cows and the NutriYum consumers is an effective satirical construction, and 'docile' is the right unexpected word that makes it land.

jokes.text: Nick Newport Jr. agrees with Leslie after the damning video — then reveals he's brought his kids Denver and Dakota to do a candy giveaway: 'Everybody! Check under your seats!'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just embarrassed Newport with the old video; Newport seems to be conceding
jokes.punchline: Newport pivots from apparent concession to a candy giveaway under the seats — an Oprah-style crowd manipulation tactic that instantly wins the crowd back, undermining Leslie's entire presentation
jokes.explanation: The Oprah-style candy giveaway as corporate counter-move is a clever satirical idea. The crowd's immediate reversal ('Look, I got chocolate!') is a perfect commentary on how easily public opinion is bought. Structurally satisfying as a Leslie defeat.

jokes.text: Leslie's aside after the candy giveaway completely works on the crowd: 'Denver, you little son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Newport's son Denver has helped distribute candy and won over the entire crowd
jokes.punchline: Leslie's muttered profanity directed at a child — which is completely out of character for her — reveals how completely she's been outmaneuvered and how frustrated she is
jokes.explanation: Perfect. Leslie Knope — who would never normally curse at a child — reaching her absolute breaking point with 'Denver, you little son of a bitch' is a great character-betrayal laugh. The name 'Denver' (the child) makes it more specific and funnier. Maximum economy, high quotability.

jokes.text: Jerry is eating NutriYums alone: 'There's no pizza left?' / 'Sorry, Jer. Too slow.' / 'Do you want my crusts? Here, take this.' / 'Nobody even told me the pizza was here.'
jokes.setup: The movers have ordered pizza for the end of the moving day
jokes.punchline: Jerry missed the pizza entirely and nobody told him — the specific cruelty of 'nobody even told me' reveals the depth of Jerry's social exclusion, which is the episode's running Jerry joke
jokes.explanation: A standard Jerry is excluded/ignored joke. 'Nobody even told me' is the specific cruelty that makes it land. Part of the established running gag about Jerry's invisibility in the office.

jokes.text: Jerry steps on DJ Roomba: 'Jerry! You stepped on DJ Roomba!' / 'That was an accident.' / 'You killed him! I built him myself. He was like a son to me.'
jokes.setup: DJ Roomba has been playing music throughout the moving day
jokes.punchline: Jerry — who missed the pizza — kills DJ Roomba by accident; Tom's grief ('He was like a son to me') is disproportionate to the destruction of a household appliance
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best payoffs. Jerry — already excluded from pizza — being the one to destroy DJ Roomba is perfect. Tom's grief is beautifully disproportionate: 'He was like a son to me' applied to a Roomba with an MP3 player is both absurd and somehow touching given Tom's established relationship with it. Strong payoff to a well-built running bit.

jokes.text: Ron frames the meeting vote with loaded language: 'All those who would like the bloated corpse of the government to keep running the snack bars at taxpayer expense, raise your hands.' / 'That seems like an unfair phrasing.' / 'And all those in favor of letting this heartless corporation, Sweetums, stuff your children with sugary crap, raise your hand.'
jokes.setup: The meeting needs to take a formal vote on the Sweetums partnership
jokes.punchline: Ron's biased framing of the government option ('bloated corpse') is so extreme that it prompts Leslie to call it unfair — then she delivers her own equally biased version ('heartless corporation... sugary crap') revealing both are doing the same thing
jokes.explanation: The parallel construction of two biased framings is structurally very well-done. Ron's 'bloated corpse of the government' is great rhetoric, and Leslie's retaliatory framing reveals her own bias in a structurally satisfying way. The setup/payoff is clean and character-specific for both characters.

jokes.text: Tom's gas-leak moving solution: 'I got it. Everybody go home, pack away my stuff in your own houses. Then on Monday, pack it back up, meet me at my new place, unload it there.'
jokes.setup: Tom's gas leak means he can't move in and he promised Wendy he'd be out — so he needs to store everything
jokes.punchline: Tom's solution — distribute his belongings among his friends' homes, then repack and move — is presented as if it's perfectly reasonable, when it doubles the work for everyone else and inconveniences everyone while solving only Tom's problem
jokes.explanation: Tom's complete obliviousness to how much extra burden he's placing on others, delivered as a brilliant solution, is good character comedy. The specificity of 'pack it back up, meet me at my new place, unload it there' makes it funnier — he's thought through his own convenience only.

jokes.text: April and Andy mock Chris (or Justin) after the move: 'Just chillaxin' like your new bro, Andy.' / 'Yeah. Wanna play some Hacky Sack later, maybe listen to Blues Traveler?' — Chris/Justin leaves: 'We're just kidding. Let's go to dinner.' — Chris: 'I'm not hungry. And you guys aren't being funny. Why are you being weird?' / 'We make fun of people like that. That's what we do.'
jokes.setup: April and Andy are mimicking Chris/Justin's overly enthusiastic bro-speak
jokes.punchline: The mockery lands poorly; their target doesn't find it funny — 'We make fun of people like that. That's what we do.' — the pair's unapologetic explanation for their cruel behavior
jokes.explanation: April and Andy as a comedy duo doing impressions of others is a nice character moment. 'That's what we do' as an explanation for cruelty is a good April line. Chillaxin/Blues Traveler as the mimicry is a slightly dated but serviceable joke.

jokes.text: Chris/Justin to April and Andy: 'You know, for a gay couple, you guys are being really gay.'
jokes.setup: Chris/Justin is irritated with April and Andy's mocking
jokes.punchline: The insult uses 'gay' as a pejorative while acknowledging they're not actually gay — the confused structure of the insult reveals it doesn't really work, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: This joke is attempting to comment on the self-defeating logic of homophobic insults, but the construction isn't quite sharp enough to fully land as satire. It's the weakest joke in the episode — the attempt at wit doesn't quite work and it's also aged somewhat poorly as humor.

jokes.text: Chris/Justin's completely uncontextualized anecdote: 'I said, "Of course I remember you. You're Chastity, right?"'
jokes.setup: Chris/Justin says this seemingly in response to being mocked, but it has no clear connection
jokes.punchline: The non-sequitur anecdote — about someone named 'Chastity' — dropped into the scene with no setup or follow-up is funny in its complete randomness and Chris's presumed confidence in its relevance
jokes.explanation: The random Chastity anecdote works as pure absurdism — the name 'Chastity' is the right kind of absurd specific — but it's underwritten. Without more context it reads as a throwaway rather than a crafted joke.

jokes.text: Ron's 'turf and turf': 'I call this "turf and turf." It's a 16-ounce T-bone and a 24-ounce porterhouse. Also, whiskey and a cigar. I'm gonna consume all of this at the same time because I am a free American.'
jokes.setup: Leslie finds Ron at dinner after his grouchy day
jokes.punchline: 'Turf and turf' — the deliberate inversion of 'surf and turf' to mean two steaks — combined with 'because I am a free American' as the justification for a performatively self-destructive meal
jokes.explanation: 'Turf and turf' is one of the series' most iconic Ron Swanson coinages. It's perfect: the inversion of 'surf and turf' that removes the sea and doubles the meat is brilliant in its simplicity. 'I am a free American' as the justification connects directly to the episode's theme of personal freedom in food choices. It's deeply character-specific (only Ron), highly original, economically perfect, and has become a genuine cultural reference point for the character. This is the episode's best joke and one of Parks and Rec's defining character moments.

jokes.text: Ron is told no cigars inside: 'Fine. I will smoke the entire thing outside.' — then immediately returns because it's freezing: 'It's freezing outside, so I will not be smoking this cigar. But rest assured, I could if I wanted to, because this... This is America, right? Is it?'
jokes.setup: Ron announces he'll smoke his cigar outside to prove his freedom
jokes.punchline: Ron's immediate capitulation to cold weather, followed by his need to maintain the ideological position while physically retreating — 'I could if I wanted to, because this... This is America, right? Is it?' — is a perfect Ron character collapse
jokes.explanation: Ron's stubbornness meeting physical reality is a great comedy structure. 'I could if I wanted to' is a classic wounded-pride dodge, and 'This is America, right? Is it?' delivered with genuine doubt by Ron Swanson — a man who has never doubted America — is a great subtle crack in the character's armor. Excellent escalation.

jokes.text: Leslie gives Ron the BAC chart back: 'So, here. Take the booze chart.' — Ron: 'Are you kidding me?' — Leslie: 'No. If you're gonna drink, you should use it, okay?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is confronting Ron about his behavior
jokes.punchline: Leslie returning the BAC chart — treating it as a genuine gift/tool — is a callback to the parking lot scene and perfectly captures Leslie's mix of practicality and earnest concern
jokes.explanation: A good structural callback that closes the BAC chart arc. Leslie's insistence on Ron using the chart ('If you're gonna drink, you should use it') is characteristically Leslie — she's not mad at the drinking, just the recklessness.

jokes.text: Leslie to Ron: 'if you eat three pounds of steak every day, you're gonna die, and although I've already written your eulogy, and it's incredibly touching, I would prefer not to give it for a while.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is expressing concern for Ron's health
jokes.punchline: Leslie has already written Ron's eulogy — and it's 'incredibly touching' — revealing both her obsessive preparation and genuine affection for Ron, while the fact that she's prepared for his death is somehow sweet
jokes.explanation: This is a great Leslie Knope joke. The pre-written eulogy is perfectly Leslie (she's prepared for everything) and the fact that it's 'incredibly touching' — as self-assessed — is funny in its immodesty. The genuine affection underneath makes it warm rather than morbid. Could only be Leslie.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals the first line of Ron's eulogy: '"O Captain! My Captain! Ron Swanson, a swan song."' / 'Yeah, and it gets better from there.'
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions she's already written Ron's eulogy
jokes.punchline: The opening line — riffing on Walt Whitman's 'O Captain! My Captain!' with a Ron/swan pun ('Swanson... swan song') — is exactly the kind of earnest, over-crafted, slightly ridiculous tribute Leslie would write. 'It gets better from there' is the button.
jokes.explanation: The Whitman riff + Swanson/swan-song pun is exactly the kind of tribute Leslie would write — literary, sincere, clever in a slightly ridiculous way. The double meaning of 'swan song' (death/farewell + swan pun) is a good wordplay construction. 'It gets better from there' — as Leslie self-assessment — is perfectly character-specific. One of the episode's strongest Leslie moments.

jokes.text: Andy rollerblades in the parking lot and tries to impress April: 'You wanna watch me rollerblade in the parking lot after work? I'm pretty awesome. I used to be really good. That was, like, 70 pounds ago.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to impress April by inviting her to watch him rollerblade
jokes.punchline: 'I used to be really good. That was, like, 70 pounds ago.' — the weight qualifier undercuts the boast and reveals Andy's physical decline with complete unselfconsciousness
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining boast structure is perfectly Andy. 'I'm pretty awesome' → 'that was 70 pounds ago' is a clean two-step. The unselfconsciousness about the weight gain is what makes it funny rather than sad — Andy has no shame about this detail.

jokes.text: Andy falls off rollerblades in front of April: 'Just kidding! I don't fall!'
jokes.setup: Andy has been trying to impress April with his rollerblading
jokes.punchline: Andy falls, then immediately denies having fallen — 'I don't fall!' — the transparent lie delivered with complete conviction after an obviously visible fall
jokes.explanation: A classic physical comedy beat. Andy's 'Just kidding! I don't fall!' is great because of his complete commitment to the denial after an obviously real fall. The '70 pounds ago' setup makes the fall funnier. Strong in-person visual gag.

jokes.text: Ron is caught eating something suspicious: 'What are you eating?' / 'I didn't have time to have breakfast.' — Ron is eating NutriYums after his entire anti-corporate-food stance
jokes.setup: Ron has spent the episode defending people's right to eat garbage while ostentatiously eating steak
jokes.punchline: Ron is secretly eating NutriYums — the very product he's defended as a matter of freedom but presumably scorns — caught with the evidence and using 'no time for breakfast' as an excuse
jokes.explanation: A nice reversal — Ron defending freedom to eat garbage, then secretly eating the garbage in question. 'I didn't have time to have breakfast' is a perfect sheepish excuse that doesn't quite cover the hypocrisy. Good character-based irony.

jokes.text: Leslie takes the NutriYums from Ron to throw them away: 'I'm gonna toss these in the dumpster outside. And I don't wanna see you digging around in there later.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confiscates Ron's NutriYums
jokes.punchline: 'I don't wanna see you digging around in there later' — the implication that Ron might actually dumpster-dive for them, which the audience believes he absolutely might do
jokes.explanation: Leslie preemptively warning Ron not to dumpster-dive implies she knows him well enough to think he'd do it — which is both funny and touches the relationship between them. The audience can absolutely imagine Ron doing exactly this.

jokes.text: Ron's apology: 'I am sorry. I have been a horse's ass. And that is the end of what I have to say.'
jokes.setup: Ron is apologizing to Leslie for his grouchy behavior
jokes.punchline: 'And that is the end of what I have to say.' — Ron's apology includes a hard stop on emotional expression. The efficiency of the apology (three sentences, done) is Ron-perfect — he acknowledges the wrong and immediately shuts down any further discussion
jokes.explanation: This is a top-tier Ron Swanson joke. 'And that is the end of what I have to say' appended to an apology is perfectly Ron — he will give the minimum required emotional content and no more. The phrase 'horse's ass' is also classically old-fashioned Ron vocabulary. The structure (apology + hard stop) is beautifully economical and reveals character perfectly. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to Ron's apology: 'Apology accepted.' — then immediately: 'Put a coat on. It's freezing outside.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered his minimal apology
jokes.punchline: Leslie accepts it without ceremony and immediately pivots to maternal concern — 'Put a coat on. It's freezing outside' — treating Ron like a child she's looking after
jokes.explanation: The pivot from emotional resolution to 'put a coat on' is perfectly Leslie — she accepts the apology with no fanfare and immediately expresses care in her most pragmatic way. The juxtaposition of the weighty apology with the mundane coat instruction is a great tonal shift. Also a callback to Ron going outside to smoke in the cold.

jokes.text: Tom's 'Ghost of DJ Roomba' confessional: 'This is the ghost of DJ Roomba. Why did you kill me? I'm gonna haunt you, Jerry. I'm gonna follow you and play the Black Eyed Peas on a non-stop loop!'
jokes.setup: Jerry has accidentally crushed DJ Roomba; Tom is doing a ghost voice for the dead robot
jokes.punchline: The 'haunt' is playing the Black Eyed Peas on a non-stop loop — a specific and inspired choice of musical torment. The 'non-stop loop' implies infinite repetition of a mildly annoying but not terrible band, which is a perfect slightly-too-much punishment for Jerry
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing joke for the DJ Roomba arc. Tom doing a ghost voice for the Roomba is wonderfully childish. 'Play the Black Eyed Peas on a non-stop loop' as the haunting is inspired — it's not death metal, it's the Black Eyed Peas, which somehow makes it worse. The non-stop loop detail seals it. A great episode-closing bit that closes multiple running threads (DJ Roomba, Jerry's exclusion/victimhood) simultaneously.

tmdb_overview: The Parks Department forms a partnership with a local company to sell energy bars at the parks in Pawnee, but Leslie tries to stop the deal when she discovers how unhealthy the snacks are. Mark reluctantly agrees to help Tom move out of his house.
insight: Sweetums corporation subplot drives 61 jokes at 2.53-per-minute pace, elevating mid-season form.
